title: Conservative stepper autoscaler with throughput reservation and emergency throttle
creator: Jordan Lee
description:
Goal: Implement a conservative-step autoscaling controller for Dedicated capacity that provides predictable throughput guarantees while minimizing oscillation and respecting fleet-level safety limits. The controller must coordinate per-tenant reservations, a small global burst pool, and an emergency throttle/circuit-breaker that gracefully degrades non-critical traffic when capacity is constrained.

Background: Current elastic policies are reactive and optimized for throughput, but we've observed oscillation during bursty workloads and occasional failures when many tenants scale simultaneously. This ticket designs and implements a conservative stepper algorithm that only changes capacity after sustained signals, enforces ramp limits, and reserves headroom for SLAs. The design is targeted at Dedicated GPU pools and integrates with the routing layer to ensure per-tenant throughput targets are met.

Target metrics and signals:
- Primary target: sustained tokens/sec per-tenant over a time window (t_window default 60s).
- Secondary signals: queue depth, 95th and 99th percentile latency, GPU utilization, and KV-cache hit ratio.
- Safety signals: cluster free GPU memory, node eviction risk, and scheduled maintenance windows.

Scaling algorithm (Conservative Stepper):
- Decision epoch: evaluate every 30s.
- Hysteresis: only consider scale-up/scale-down after threshold exceeded for N consecutive epochs (default N=3 for scale-up, N=5 for scale-down).
- Step size: capacity changes in discrete steps (e.g., 1, 2, 4 GPU-equivalents) determined by a step matrix tuned per instance-type.
- Ramp limit: max increase 8 GPUs / 10m and max decrease 12 GPUs / 10m per pool to avoid cascading evictions.
- Headroom reservation: maintain a configurable headroom percentage (default 10%) of pool capacity reserved for SLA-bound tenants. Reservations are enforced by pre-allocating tokens in the routing layer.
- Burst pool: small shared burst pool (configurable, default 5% of pool) for absorbing short spikes; immediate but short TTL allocations (60s).

Safety controls and fallback behaviors:
- Emergency throttle: when cluster-level free capacity < safety_threshold (5%) and eviction risk rising, throttle non-SLA routes by progressively dropping best-effort requests or routing to cheaper model variants. Throttling uses a token-bucket per-route to avoid synchronized drops.
- Circuit breaker: if scale failures or API errors cross a severity threshold, automatically stop scale-out attempts and trigger on-call page + telemetry alert.
- Backpressure to clients: return structured backpressure responses via the API (503 with retry-after header + structured reason code) where applicable.

Cross-tenant fairness:
- Enforce per-tenant max concurrency and proportional fairness for burst pool consumption based on committed reservation and historical usage.
- Soft limits for new tenants: new tenants start in a restricted mode until they pass a warm-up traffic profile to avoid noisy neighbor startup spikes.

Observability and telemetry:
- Expose decision-level traces: epoch input signals, chosen action, reason codes, and safety limit hits.
- Dashboards: per-pool scaling events, step size histogram, oscillation index (new metric), and headroom usage.
- Alerts: p95 latency regressions post-scale, repeated emergency throttle events, and repeated scale failure retries.

Simulations & results:
- Ran offline simulations on 2025-Q4 production traces and worst-case synthetic spikes. Conservative Stepper reduced oscillation (defined as >2 scale events in a 5m window) by ~62% and reduced eviction incidents by 87% at the cost of +3% committed GPU-hours in tail scenarios.
- Simulation notebooks: include parameter sweeps for step size, hysteresis windows, and ramp limits. The chosen defaults represent a trade-off between cost and SLA stability.

Rollout plan:
1) Canary: 1 pool in us-west-2 with read-only policy for 48h (collection only).
2) Small live canary: enable for a set of low-risk tenants with feature flag, run 1 week.
3) Gradual ramp: enable for additional pools/tenants while tracking oscillation index and our telemetry SLOs.
4) Full enable: after 4 weeks with stable metrics, flip default policy and remove flag.

Backward compatibility: Controller will expose an opt-in flag per pool. Default behavior remains unchanged until full enable. Routing integration will use capability negotiation so older routing agents fall back to previous allocation logic.
comments: 2026-02-19: Kickoff meeting notes added. Agreed on primary metrics and that headroom must be enforceable from routing. (See confluence: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Conservative+Stepper+Autoscaler)
2026-02-25: Simulation 1 completed; step size 2 produced frequent small oscillations. Increased hysteresis to N=3 for scale-up. Notebook: https://drive.redwood.ai/simulations/stepper-v1.ipynb

2026-03-01: Design review with Marco Ruiz and SRE. Feedback: tighten ramp limits and add an explicit emergency throttle circuit. Action: add token-bucket throttle and integrate with routing reasons. Recording: https://meetings.redwood.ai/rec/2026-03-01-stepper-review

2026-03-04: PR opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/12345 (controller + tests). Reviewers requested clearer metrics tagging and one end-to-end integration test. Assigned to Aisha for follow-up.

2026-03-08: QA found a race when multiple pools request growth simultaneously leading to temporary overcommit; mitigated by central allocator lock and optimistic reservation. Patch in PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/12368
2026-03-09: Observability dashboards prototype available: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/AVC2X-stepper; added oscillation-index panel and headroom usage heatmap.
acceptance_criteria: Controller implements conservative stepper algorithm with configurable hysteresis and step matrix
Headroom reservation enforced by routing and visible in telemetry
Emergency throttle and circuit-breaker implemented with documented behavior and reason codes
Automated tests for race conditions and central allocator locking
Simulation results reproduced in CI notebooks and baseline comparison attached
Dashboards and alerts deployed for canary pool before live enablement
decisions: Use tokens/sec as primary scaling signal rather than instantaneous GPU utilization to prefer user-visible throughput stability
Discrete step-size matrix over continuous scaling to reduce frequent small adjustments
Reserve 10% headroom by default to prioritize SLA-bound tenants; configurable per-customer
Include a tiny shared burst pool to absorb short spikes without triggering scale-out
notes: Trade-off: more conservative scaling increases short-term cost under sustained load but reduces customer-visible latency spikes and evictions
We chose longer hysteresis for scale-down to avoid flip-flop on intermittent drops; this increases tail cost if load permanently drops quickly
Security review required because controller can affect routing decisions and tenant isolation; compliance with KMS/audit flows must be preserved
Next: coordinate with Console team to display per-tenant reservation and throttle reasons in the UI
